strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-resourced problem: open-vocabulary affordance grounding in both 3D and 2D. As a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, the proposed Affogato dataset is substantial in scale, with 150K 3D objects, 750K query-heatmap pairs, projected 2D supervision, and broader category/affordance coverage than prior affordance datasets.

The automated Affogato-Engine pipeline is practical and well motivated: using VLM-based query generation, point grounding, SAM-based masks, and multi-view lifting/voting is a plausible way to scale affordance annotation beyond manual labeling. The paper also reports human quality assessment and manual refinement for the test split, which strengthens the benchmark case.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for this contribution type. The paper evaluates 3D cross-dataset transfer, cross-domain open-vocabulary generalization, zero-shot 2D transfer to AGD20K, and fine-tuning performance. The results consistently suggest that Affogato pretraining improves generalization and can outperform heavier VLM/LLM-based baselines in 2D affordance grounding.

The work is not merely a dataset dump: the Espresso-2D and Espresso-3D baselines provide simple, reproducible model recipes and demonstrate that the dataset contains usable supervision signals. The inclusion of failure cases, limitations, partial-view experiments, and annotation-quality discussion is helpful.

The paper is generally clear and well organized, with strong motivation, useful comparisons to prior datasets, and a convincing argument that existing 3D affordance datasets are narrow and sometimes noisy.
weaknesses: The central risk is annotation validity. Only 1K objects / 5K query-heatmap pairs are manually assessed out of 750K pairs, and 15.4% are rated 'not good' even in this sample. Since the training set appears largely automatically generated and unrefined, the paper does not fully establish how much label noise remains or how it affects downstream learning.

The benchmark may partially evaluate agreement with the same automated annotation process used to create the data. Although the test split is inspected and bad examples are refined, much of the supervision and evaluation protocol still depends on VLM/SAM-generated heatmaps. More independent human-labeled evaluation, especially on unseen real objects/scenes, would make the scientific case stronger.

The claimed open-vocabulary generalization is promising but not fully stress-tested. Cross-domain splits within Affogato and transfer to LASO/AGD20K are useful, but the paper provides limited analysis of genuinely novel interaction concepts, ambiguous prompts, compositional instructions, or real-world robotic/embodied use cases beyond contact heatmaps.

Some experimental comparisons are difficult to interpret. Absolute 3D aIoU values on Affogato are low, MAE is acknowledged as unreliable across annotation protocols, and the LASO-versus-Affogato cross-dataset table mixes datasets with different annotation styles and quality. This supports the dataset's utility but weakens precise claims about model superiority.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in places. The abstract says the dataset is shared publicly but the link appears missing in the provided manuscript. The exact prompts, filtering criteria, licensing/redistribution constraints inherited from Objaverse/G-Objaverse, and full annotation pipeline implementation details would be important for a dataset paper.

The paper relies heavily on large pretrained foundation models whose biases, failure modes, and hallucinations may shape the generated affordance distribution. The societal/data-bias discussion is relatively light, particularly given the use of web-crawled 3D assets and generated interaction descriptions.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck for affordance grounding: the lack of large-scale, open-vocabulary 3D/2D supervision. A dataset of 150K Objaverse assets and 750K query-heatmap pairs would be useful if released with sufficient documentation and quality controls.

The proposed data engine is pragmatic and scalable, combining VLM query generation, point grounding, SAM masks, and multi-view aggregation. The pipeline is simple but plausible, and the paper provides implementation details and some failure-mode analysis.

The work evaluates both 3D and 2D affordance grounding, including cross-dataset transfer to LASO and zero-shot/fine-tuning experiments on AGD20K. The reported 2D gains after Affogato pretraining suggest the generated data may provide useful supervision.
The authors acknowledge some limitations, including lack of real backgrounds, ambiguity in 2D affordance labels, and failures of the automated annotation pipeline.
weaknesses: The contribution is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper rather than an Algorithms/General paper. Under that standard, the central weakness is insufficient evidence that the generated annotations are reliable at scale. Only 5K pairs from 1K objects are human-rated, 15.4% are judged 'not good', and there is no inter-annotator agreement, sampling protocol detail, expert qualification detail, or category-wise breakdown. This is a serious concern for a dataset whose main claim is high-quality automatic annotation.

The training split appears to retain noisy automatically generated annotations, while the test split is manually filtered/refined. This creates a potentially optimistic benchmark: models are evaluated on a cleaned subset, but the claimed dataset quality applies to the much larger unverified corpus. The paper does not quantify how noise affects training or provide ablations over annotation quality.

The benchmark validation is somewhat circular. Much of the 3D evaluation is on Affogato’s own generated labels, and the paper also argues that prior human datasets such as LASO/3D AffordanceNet are flawed. This leaves limited independent evidence that Affogato improves real affordance understanding rather than fitting the biases of Gemma/Molmo/SAM and the aggregation pipeline.

The 'open-vocabulary' claim is overextended. The experiments mostly test transfer across object subsets or existing affordance datasets, but do not provide a rigorous held-out affordance/query split, compositional language evaluation, synonym robustness analysis, or evaluation on genuinely novel interaction concepts.

The Espresso models are mostly straightforward combinations of existing pretrained encoders and transformer-style decoders. This is acceptable for a dataset paper, but the algorithmic novelty is limited, and some claims about the frozen-encoder strategy are not backed by sufficiently detailed ablations in the main paper.

The 2D comparisons are not fully satisfying. Espresso is trained on a large task-specific generated dataset, while several baselines are generic VLM/segmentation models or results adopted from prior work under potentially different protocols. The paper needs stronger controlled baselines, for example training comparable architectures on alternative synthetic data, Molmo/SAM pseudo-labels directly, or smaller Affogato subsets.

Several methodological details needed for reproducibility and trust are underspecified: exact prompts, filtering rules, heatmap projection/voting parameters, object selection criteria, licensing/attribution handling for Objaverse assets, and the public release link appears missing/blank in the abstract.

The societal/benchmark limitations are underdeveloped. Because the dataset is derived from web-crawled 3D assets and foundation-model outputs, it may inherit category, cultural, and functional biases; these are not meaningfully audited. For embodied use, contact heatmaps alone also omit pose, force, stability, safety, and physical feasibility, yet the paper’s framing sometimes suggests broader affordance understanding than the evidence supports.

strengths: The paper is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution rather than a primarily algorithmic one: its main value is the Affogato dataset and automated annotation pipeline, with Espresso serving as a deliberately simple validation model. Under that framing, the scale and breadth are compelling: 150K 3D assets, 750K query-heatmap pairs, >450 object classes and >350 affordance concepts, plus aligned 2D renderings, substantially exceed prior 3D affordance grounding resources.

The proposed Affogato-Engine is a practical and well-motivated way to exploit modern VLMs and segmentation models for scalable affordance annotation. The multi-view pointing, SAM-based mask generation, and 2D-to-3D voting aggregation are conceptually simple but appropriate for generating dense affordance heatmaps at scale.

The manuscript provides useful validation beyond dataset statistics. The 1K-object/5K-pair human quality audit, refinement of poor test annotations, cross-dataset evaluation against LASO, cross-domain Affogato splits, and 2D transfer to AGD20K together make a credible case that the dataset provides transferable supervision rather than merely synthetic labels.

The 2D results are particularly convincing: Espresso-2D pretrained on Affogato improves zero-shot AGD20K performance over Molmo+SAM/LISA/M2SA and improves fully supervised AGD20K fine-tuning results over the non-pretrained version, supporting the claim that the generated data is useful outside its own benchmark.

The paper is clear and well organized, with helpful comparisons to existing datasets, qualitative examples, implementation details, failure-mode discussion, and partial-view experiments in the appendix. The authors also acknowledge important limitations, such as contact-point-only supervision and missing real scene context.
weaknesses: The strongest evidence is still partly circular: the main 3D benchmark is generated by the proposed pipeline, and only the test split is manually checked/refined. Since the training set remains automatically generated and the human audit reports 15.4% 'not good' annotations, the paper would be stronger with more systematic quality statistics, inter-annotator agreement, and error rates broken down by object type, affordance type, and visibility condition.

The paper’s public-release and reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript text. The abstract appears to leave the dataset URL blank, and important release details such as asset filtering criteria, license constraints inherited from Objaverse/G-Objaverse, exact prompts, post-processing thresholds, train/validation/test splits, and annotation confidence calibration are not fully specified in the main paper.

The Espresso architecture is intentionally simple, which is acceptable for a dataset paper, but the 3D experimental comparison is somewhat narrow. Only OpenAD and PointRefer are used as main 3D baselines, and the paper does not extensively compare against stronger recent open-vocabulary 3D segmentation or affordance models beyond adapting a few baselines. This limits confidence about how broadly the benchmark ranks methods.

Absolute 3D grounding performance remains fairly low in several settings, especially cross-domain Daily-used/Furnitures transfer where aIoU can be below 0.05 in one direction. The authors frame this as a challenging open-vocabulary setting, which is reasonable, but it also suggests the task/dataset may still contain substantial ambiguity or noise not fully characterized by the current metrics.

The evaluation of real-world embodied relevance is limited. Affogato predicts contact-region heatmaps, but not grasp pose, force, action trajectory, object state, or task success, and it is derived from isolated Objaverse objects without scene context. The authors acknowledge this, but it constrains the practical impact claims for robotics and embodied AI.

Some claims about prior dataset quality and Affogato superiority rely on qualitative examples and aggregate coverage/diversity measures whose definitions may not fully capture semantic correctness. Higher heatmap coverage/diversity is not always better if multiple regions are implausible, so these analyses should be interpreted cautiously.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck for affordance grounding: the lack of large, open-vocabulary 3D/2D supervision. Framing the work primarily as a datasets/benchmarks contribution is appropriate, and the scale of Affogato-750K is a meaningful contribution relative to existing affordance datasets.

The automated annotation pipeline is technically sensible: query generation, point grounding, SAM-based mask generation, and multi-view 2D-to-3D aggregation are combined in a coherent way, with explicit error mitigation and failure-mode analysis.

The authors provide useful empirical evidence that the dataset is not just large but transferable: pretraining improves multiple 3D methods on LASO unseen splits, improves 2D zero-shot and fine-tuned AGD20K results, and shows monotonic benefits from increased pretraining scale in the supplement.

The 5K human-verified test split, held-out instance/query/view construction, category-filtering analysis, and cross-domain evaluations are good steps toward reliable benchmarking rather than only reporting in-domain performance.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with useful qualitative visualizations and a simple unified Espresso baseline that helps separate dataset value from architectural novelty.
weaknesses: The central training set remains automatically generated and only partially validated. The reported 84.8% success rate implies nontrivial label noise, but the paper does not provide enough quantitative analysis of how this noise affects training, whether failure rates vary across object/affordance types, or whether annotator agreement is reliable.

The semantic diversity claims depend on Gemma-predicted object and affordance labels rather than a human-normalized taxonomy, so the reported >450 classes and >350 affordances may overstate true coverage due to synonymy, inconsistent granularity, or misclassification.

The dataset release/reproducibility story is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the supplementary section titled “Dataset link” is blank, and there is little discussion of Objaverse asset licensing, filtering, annotation storage format, or whether generated labels/heatmaps and code will be released.

Evaluation on real-world embodied settings is still limited. The Open X-Embodiment result is qualitative only, and the main quantitative 2D transfer still relies on AGD20K; this leaves uncertainty about how well the synthetic isolated-object supervision supports cluttered scenes, occlusions, and robot-relevant interaction constraints.

Some comparisons are hard to fully interpret because the baselines use different pretraining histories and architectures, and Espresso relies on strong pretrained encoders. The paper does include prior-method pretraining experiments, but a more controlled cost/compute and backbone-matched comparison would strengthen the causal case for the dataset.

The proposed Espresso architectures are intentionally simple and only modestly novel, so the acceptance case rests mainly on the dataset. The benchmark itself also shows large remaining headroom and asymmetric cross-domain behavior, suggesting that the generated data distribution is still biased toward certain Objaverse subsets.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck for affordance grounding: the lack of large-scale open-vocabulary supervision, especially in 3D. As a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, the scale of Affogato-750K and the attempt to connect 3D and 2D affordance grounding are potentially valuable.

The automated pipeline is conceptually reasonable: using a VLM for query generation, a pointing model for interaction localization, SAM-style segmentation, and multi-view voting to lift 2D signals into 3D heatmaps. The paper also includes useful analyses of failure modes, data scale, background augmentation, and held-out category filtering.

Experiments show that pretraining on Affogato-750K often improves transfer, especially on unseen LASO settings and AGD20K, and the gains are demonstrated for both the proposed Espresso models and some prior methods. This supports the claim that the generated data contains transferable supervision.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with helpful qualitative examples and a broad comparison to existing affordance datasets.
weaknesses: The central claim of reliable large-scale automatic annotation is not fully convincing. The reported 84.8% success rate on 5K samples implies substantial noise, but the paper does not give enough detail about the rating protocol, inter-annotator agreement, pass/fail thresholds, or how representative the sample is across object categories and affordance types. For a dataset paper, this is a major weakness.

The test split is human-verified/refined, while the training set remains automatically generated. This is sensible for evaluation, but it also means the paper does not adequately quantify the quality of the actual 750K training annotations beyond a small validation sample and qualitative comparisons.

The evaluation of the new Affogato-750K benchmark is somewhat circular: models are trained and tested on data from the same synthetic Objaverse/G-Objaverse generation pipeline, and the benchmark may reward adaptation to the pipeline’s biases rather than real-world affordance understanding. The real-world evidence is mostly qualitative.

Some claims are overstated. Pretraining is described as consistently beneficial, but Table 2 shows degradations for some seen-setting metrics and worse MAE for Espresso-3D after pretraining. The improvements are real in places, but the conclusions should be more nuanced.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a dataset/benchmark submission. Appendix A is just a placeholder for a dataset link, prompts are not fully specified, and the filtering analysis relies on Gemma judgments without enough validation. Licensing/usage issues for Objaverse-derived assets and generated annotations are also not discussed in adequate detail.

There are internal inconsistencies and presentation issues. For example, the main text says Espresso-3D finetunes both the 3D vision encoder and text encoder, while the appendix says the vision backbone is frozen. Figures/tables also contain formatting artifacts and occasional naming inconsistencies, which reduce confidence in the experimental reporting.

The Espresso models are mostly straightforward adaptations of existing encoders and decoder designs, so the algorithmic novelty is limited. This is acceptable for a dataset paper, but it increases the burden on dataset quality, benchmark design, and reproducibility, where the current submission still has important gaps.

The limitations section is too narrow. It mentions missing backgrounds but does not seriously discuss synthetic asset bias, nonphysical or low-quality Objaverse objects, culturally variable affordances, safety-sensitive affordances, ambiguous language-object grounding, or downstream robotic misuse/failure risks.

strengths: The paper presents a strong Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, even though the contribution type is not explicitly declared. Affogato-750K addresses a clear bottleneck in affordance grounding by providing 750K open-vocabulary query-heatmap annotations over 150K Objaverse objects, with both 3D and projected 2D supervision.

The proposed automated annotation pipeline is sensible and well motivated: Gemma3 generates function-oriented queries, Molmo predicts interaction points, MobileSAM converts points to masks, and multi-view voting aggregates 2D evidence into 3D heatmaps. The paper also includes practical error-mitigation choices such as chain-of-thought prompting, smallest-mask selection, and multi-view consensus.

The empirical evidence is broad and convincing for the central claim that the dataset is useful supervision. Pretraining on Affogato-750K improves multiple 3D methods on LASO unseen splits, improves Espresso-3D on the authors' own held-out test split, and gives strong 2D transfer to AGD20K in zero-shot and supervised settings.

The authors make a meaningful effort to validate dataset quality. They report a 5K human-verified test split, an 84.8% success rate for automatically generated pairs before correction, common failure modes, held-out category filtering, scale ablations, resolution analysis, and qualitative comparisons to human annotations.

The paper is clear and well organized. The motivation, dataset pipeline, model design, evaluation protocols, and limitations are easy to follow, and the work is likely to be useful to researchers in affordance grounding, 3D vision-language learning, and embodied AI.
weaknesses: The strongest concern is label quality in the training set. The human validation suggests about 15.2% of sampled automatic annotations fail before correction, but the large training split appears to remain automatically generated. The paper would be stronger with more detailed quality control statistics, inter-annotator agreement, and estimates of residual noise across object domains and affordance types.

The automated labels inherit biases and failure modes from Gemma3, Molmo, and MobileSAM. Incorrect object recognition, semantically implausible affordance queries, point-localization errors, and SAM edge bias are acknowledged, but the paper does not deeply quantify how these biases affect downstream models beyond aggregate performance.

The dataset is large but source diversity is limited: it is built from isolated Objaverse/G-Objaverse assets in four selected categories, with clean synthetic renderings and no real backgrounds, clutter, occlusion, articulated object state, human hands, or scene context. This limits how directly the benchmark measures real embodied interaction in natural environments.

The claim of open-vocabulary affordance coverage is plausible but partly dependent on model-generated class and affordance descriptions. Counts such as >450 object classes and >350 affordances are derived from predictions/frequencies rather than a human-curated ontology, so semantic redundancy, ambiguity, and long-tail quality remain uncertain.

Some reproducibility details are incomplete. The appendix has a 'Dataset link' heading but the extracted manuscript text does not show an actual link, and generating the dataset requires several large pretrained models and substantial GPU resources. Public release of generated annotations, prompts, code, and exact filtering/splitting scripts is important for the contribution to be fully reproducible.

The Espresso models are useful baselines, but the algorithmic novelty is modest. This is acceptable for a dataset/benchmark paper, yet the paper should avoid over-emphasizing the models as a major standalone contribution relative to the dataset and data engine.
